newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cautiously hopeful on Russian space promise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cautiously hopeful on Russian space promise.

text.p: U.S. officials expressed guarded optimism on Wednesday that cash-strapped Russia will come up on time with the money it has promised to stay as a partner in the international space station project.

Daniel Goldin, chief of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and John Gibbons, White House director of science, tried to reassure sceptical members of the House of Representatives Science Committee that Russia will meet its obligations as promised by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin last week in meetings with Vice President Al Gore.

Under the plan, Russia, which one congressman described as "an economic basket case," was to provide $100 million by the end of this month and $250 million by the end of the year toward building a key component, called a service module, so the space station project can go forward.
Russia earlier said it was way behind schedule because of money problems which could delay the start of the space station project further or even jeopardise the project itself.
So far the United States has spent $18 billion toward the joint international project, which has been in the works since 1984.
The first in a series of launches to build the space station was scheduled for November if Russia comes up with money to complete the service module. If it does not, there could be a delay.

A second launch of a component for the station was scheduled for a month later and the Russian service module component had been scheduled for launch in April 1998 before the delays from lack of funding.
The module would include crew quarters and key naviation and guidance equipment.
If Russia does not keep its money promises, the U.S. officials said there were contingency plans including using some existing U.S. hardware until the Russian service module is delivered.
Goldin told the subcommittee that "we have come to a critical juncture" in dealing with the Russian government.
"We now have a very specific commitment from the Russian government, citing specific amounts and dates," Goldin said.
"While I am cautiously optimistic that, this time, the commitment will result in funding, we will take action based only on observed performance, not on mere statements of intent," he said.

Similarly Gibbons said, "We are optimistic that the prime minister will deliver on his commitment. We will be looking very closely at whether the Russian Space Agency receives the promised funding by the end of the month."
Marcia Smith, an official of the Congressional Research Service which does research for Congress, was more pessimistic.

She said Russia was technically capable of meeting the commitment to be a full partner in the space station but "the question is whether the Russian government will provide the requisite funding. Today Russia is having difficulty supporting its own space station, Mir, despite substantial payments from the United States and European countries."
